Core editing

  • Enter / F2 → edit
  • Enter → new sibling below (while editing)
  • Shift + Enter → split at the cursor — text after the cursor moves into a new sibling below, text before it stays put
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Enter → new child — works whether you're editing a node or just have one selected
  • Type → start editing

Navigation

  • Click → select
  • Shift + Click → range
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Click → multi-select
  • Ctrl/Cmd + A → select all

Quick Assist

  • Lives in the header, where a plain search box used to sit. Ctrl/Cmd + K focuses it and opens the results dropdown from anywhere in the app; clicking directly into the box does the same. Type a plain-English instruction and it's carried out immediately: "get me toolbar," "I don't want file explorer," "toggle dark mode" — or just type anything else to search documents, notes, tags, settings, and help. Not to be confused with Quick Insert (Ctrl/Cmd + Space) — a much smaller character-insert menu that opens instead whenever you're actively editing text, described below
  • An empty box shows a "Try things like…" tip with a handful of example phrases — click any of them to run it as a search immediately, same as typing it yourself; nothing executes without a second click on the actual result.
  • To search just one category instead of all of them at once, type a category prefix before your query — "notes: budget" only searches Notes, "settings: dark" only searches Settings. Short aliases work too (doc/docs, note/notes, tag/tags, and so on). Threads and Diagrams each have their own prefix too — "thread: EDI" (or "comment:", "question:", "discussion:", "qa:") searches only thread entries (text, Yes/No, author and context), "diagram: flow" only Diagrams (title + note). "table: Berlin" searches only table cells and table titles (the result shows the matching row), "image: login" only image captions. Don't want to remember the exact word? Click the icon at the left of the box, or press Space while it's completely empty — either shows a picker inline in the dropdown, navigable the same way search results are (↓ / ↑ to move, Enter to pick). Above the categories, the same picker also lists Show, Hide, Toggle, and Run — picking one inserts that bare word instead of a category prefix, which does something different: rather than scoping a search, it browses everything of that kind (see the bare-verb bullet below). Either way, choosing an entry leaves the dropdown open, cursor ready for you to keep typing and narrow further. A category prefix with nothing typed after it (just "notes: " on its own) shows no results rather than browsing the whole category — the box doesn't have a "show me everything in here" mode for categories, only "search within here," so you still need something to search for after a category prefix specifically; the four verb words above are the exception; each of those does browse everything on its own with nothing else typed
  • Typing just a bare word — "show," "hide," "toggle," or "run," nothing else — lists everything of that kind instead of requiring you to already know a specific setting's name: "show" lists everything currently hidden that could be shown, "hide" lists everything currently shown that could be hidden, "toggle" lists everything either way regardless of its current state, and "run" lists every available Run action ("new document," "duplicate node," and the AI actions covered below). Keep typing after the bare word to narrow the list further by name — "show file" narrows to just File Explorer-related results, the same as typing "show file explorer" would, just built up in two steps instead of one
  • On a Mac, if the system's own Spotlight is bound to Cmd+Space (its default), it takes priority over the browser and this shortcut won't fire — either change Spotlight's shortcut in macOS System Settings → Keyboard, or remap this one from Settings → Keyboard Shortcuts
  • Toggles and search are rule-based, not AI — a fixed set of recognized phrases (show/get/enable/turn on… vs. hide/remove/get rid of/turn off…) matched against a fixed list of settings. Nothing is sent anywhere for these, no API key needed, and it never improvises — if it doesn't recognize a phrase, it says so rather than guessing. The AI Run actions below are the one exception: those do call your configured AI provider, the same as clicking their toolbar/right-click equivalent would
  • Covers the everyday visibility toggles: file explorer (and its filter box), zen mode, dark/light mode, auto-rewrite on commit, spellcheck, backlinks, outline numbering, the Quick Assist search box itself and its icon-only mode, icon-only Import/Export in the app bar, accent-colored branches, and the startup tab/blank-session preferences — plus the on/off switches for AI Capabilities, Focus, and Backlinks. It does not cover destructive actions (reset, delete, empty trash) or multi-value settings (themes, sliders) — those still live in Settings, on purpose
  • The capability switches are reachable with a slightly longer phrase than you might expect — "focus feature", "backlinks feature", "ai capabilities" — rather than their bare names. That's deliberate: a bare word like "focus" is also something Quick Assist searches for as content, so a short keyword there would rank a toggle above the search hit you were actually looking for.
  • Below command matches, a separate row type labeled Run covers one-off actions instead of toggles: "new document," "duplicate node," and "duplicate" — or type the bare word "run" with nothing else to list all of them at once, the same way a bare "show" or "hide" lists every matching toggle. These don't have an on/off state to show or an existing value to report — they just do the thing once, the same as clicking the equivalent toolbar or Settings button would. Only safe, additive, undoable operations are ever reachable this way; nothing destructive is offered as a Run action, same rule as the toggles above. "Duplicate node" needs a node selected first — if nothing's selected, it still shows up (so you know it exists) but greyed out with "select a node first" instead of a working button, rather than either hiding it or letting a click do nothing unexplained. Undo is the regular document Undo
  • AI Run actions — also listed under "run," these are the exception to "rule-based, not AI" above: "rewrite this node" / "rewrite selected" (current selection, single or multiple nodes), and "generate outline" (opens the same topic-prompt dialog as its toolbar button). Each needs an API key configured in Settings → AI → Provider and disappears entirely if AI Capabilities (Settings → AI) is off — same requirement as the toolbar buttons they reuse. Unlike the rule-based actions above, these take a moment to run and can fail (expired key, provider rate limit) exactly like clicking their toolbar equivalent would — a missing key or a failed call surfaces the same error dialog either way, not a silent no-op. Undo works the regular way once a result lands, since each reuses the exact same function — and therefore the exact same pushUndo() call — as its toolbar/right-click counterpart
  • Below any command and action matches, the same box also surfaces matching documents, node text, notes, tags, folders, each document's Q&A, Diagrams, and Remarks, plus To-Dos, and settings/help topics. These rows are labeled Go to instead of Show/Hide, since picking one navigates you there rather than changing anything, and each shows a short snippet of where the match sits so you're not guessing what you're about to open
  • Clicking a "Go to" result does the right thing for its type: a node-text match jumps to that node and highlights the match; a Notes match expands that node's inline note and focuses it; a Tags match jumps to the tagged node; a Q&A or Remarks match opens that document, expands the node it's linked to, and puts the cursor in it (unlinked ones, which have nowhere to be shown, are left out); a Diagrams match opens that specific diagram; a To-Dos match opens the Hub to that entry
  • Skips Trash by default. Settings → Trash → "Include Trash in search" surfaces matches there too, across every content type above, clearly marked "In Trash"; clicking one reveals it in the Trash section rather than opening it directly, since restoring is a deliberate choice
  • Rich-text fields (Notes, Q&A, Remarks) are stripped to plain text before matching, so a search never hits raw HTML markup and snippets always show readable text
  • The file explorer's own filter box only matches document names, not their contents — for anything inside a document, this box is the one that actually looks
  • Every document has a status chip — No status by default, or Draft, Review, Approved, Rejected — next to the title field. Click it to open a small menu and pick one; it's a menu rather than a cycle-through-in-order control like the diagram status chip, since jumping straight to the one you want beats clicking past the others first. Existing documents start with no status until you set one; it's never assumed. Duplicating a document resets its copy to No status rather than carrying the original's over, same reasoning as why the title gets "(copy)" appended instead of reused verbatim — a fresh copy hasn't itself been through review or approval. Version History restores status alongside everything else for versions saved after this feature shipped; older versions predating it simply leave the current status untouched on restore rather than guessing
  • Settings → Bars & Menus → Quick Assist → "Quick Assist search box" shows or hides the box itself — Ctrl/Cmd + K opens and focuses it either way
  • As you type, the list runs in a fixed order top to bottom — matching commands first, then Run actions, then search results — each labeled with what it'll do ("Hide File Explorer," "Turn on Zen mode," "Run: New document," "Go to: …") and, for toggles, the setting's current state; ↓ / ↑ moves through the combined list (disabled Run rows are skipped, since there's nothing to activate), Enter runs or opens whichever is highlighted, Esc closes and clears the box, or click any of them directly
  • Every command and Run action shows a toast with an Undo button — nothing is ever silently applied. Just typing a bare toggle name with no verb ("zen mode," "file explorer") flips its current state rather than doing nothing. If a Run action has its own confirmation step and you cancel that step, nothing happens and the toast says so instead of falsely claiming success. "Go to" rows are navigation, not a change to anything, so there's nothing to undo for those
  • If a phrase matches more than one setting, all of them show up as separate ranked options instead of Quick Assist silently picking one for you

Quick Insert

  • Ctrl/Cmd + Space while actively editing any text — a node, a Note, a To-Do, anywhere — opens a small character-insert menu. Same shortcut, same menu, everywhere you're editing text; the full Quick Assist is a separate shortcut (Ctrl/Cmd + K) and stays free even mid-edit, so the two are never in competition for the same key
  • Actions, in order: Insert em dash, Insert en dash, Insert arrow, Insert check mark, Insert cross mark, Insert middle dot, Insert date/time. Which of these appear (and their fixed order) is configured in Settings → Editing → Quick Insert → Menu items
  • No typeahead — unlike @mentions or the full Quick Assist, this menu doesn't filter as you type. ↓ / ↑ moves through it and wraps at either end, Enter runs the highlighted action, Esc or resuming normal typing dismisses it. There's deliberately nowhere for a typed query to live except the text you're editing, which this avoids touching
  • Every action splices directly at the cursor and keeps you in edit mode, so you don't lose your place — the fastest way to get these in, and the reason the menu exists
  • Node-only actions — Note, Tags, Thread, Rewrite node, Version history — live in a node's right-click menu instead, not here, since Quick Insert is deliberately the same small menu everywhere rather than growing extra items only inside the outline editor
  • Version history… (right-click a node → in the "notes" group of the More panel) — shows earlier text for just this one node, drawn from the document's regular version history (captured automatically roughly every 10 minutes of active changes — see the Version History entry below) — skips straight past versions where this particular node didn't change, so a document with 20 saved versions might show far fewer than 20 rows here. "Restore text" replaces only this node's text, through the normal undo stack (Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes it like any other edit) — nothing else about the node (note, code, tags) is touched

Appearance & Display

  • Theme & accent — Settings → Appearance: Light/Dark theme and six accent colours (Terracotta, the default, plus Teal, Indigo, Violet, Moss, and Amber). Auto theme sits below it — Off (the Light/Dark switch only, changed by hand) or System (follows your OS/browser's dark mode setting live). Manually clicking Light/Dark in System mode holds as a temporary override until the system value naturally catches up and agrees with it again
  • Status bar — always shown, including in zen mode: word count and current depth on the left; on the right, saved status, the Secure Storage lock chip (only while locked), the auto-rewrite indicator (while auto-rewrite is on), and Quick Assist when it's docked there
  • App bar — always shown, including in zen mode, so Settings is always one click away. "Declutter app bar" (in the app bar's own right-click menu) hides the title field, file explorer toggle, and Documents/Templates buttons
  • Toolbar — always shown above the editor (hidden only in zen mode), one fixed set of buttons in unlabeled groups: Undo, Redo · Outdent, Indent · Bold, Italic, Highlight (with its colour picker), Text colour (with its picker), Heading style · Note, Checkbox, Tags · Generate outline, Rewrite node (AI) — and Collapse all + Zoom as a small pair at the right end. It wraps onto a second line on a narrow window rather than scrolling. Everything else — Insert above/below, Add child, Duplicate, Move up/down, Delete — is in a node's right-click menu (and the keyboard shortcuts below); Underline, Strikethrough, and Insert date/time are keyboard shortcuts
  • The tree always renders in a clean indented view, closer to Dynalist or Workflowy — no │├└─ connector characters. Every row gets a small dot instead of a triangle fold-arrow — a folded parent shows as a ring with a dot inside, hovering either kind reveals −/+ — plus a faint vertical guide line per indent level so nesting stays easy to trace. This isn't a setting; it's the app's only tree style
  • Text size — Settings → Appearance → Text size: a slider from 85% to 140%
  • All of the above are saved automatically and restored next time you open the app. "Reset to default settings" (Settings → Data) reverts appearance and behaviour preferences to their defaults without touching your documents

Structure

  • Right-click a node → a small row of marker icons (Agreed, Follow-up, Out of scope — see the Markers entry below) sits above everything else; below that, a fixed row of icon buttons for the most common actions: Rewrite, Note, Add comment, Add question, Add diagram, Add table. Click More for everything else — Insert above/below, Add child, Duplicate, Zoom in, Move up/down, Collapse/expand, Sort children, Add image, Tags, Generate diagram, Insert date/time, Version history, and Delete. Zoom in is also in the toolbar and via Ctrl/Cmd + .; zoom out via Ctrl/Cmd + , or clicking the same toolbar button again
  • Markers — three quick marks (✓ Agreed, ⚑ Follow-up, ⊘ Out of scope) for tracking status on a node, e.g. while reviewing a document. Each one is the node's thread status: setting a marker records it in the thread, by you, now (starting the thread if there is none; Follow-up also opens the reply line, to say what's left), and a status set in the thread sets the marker — the two always agree. Older documents' Issue rows read as Follow-up and N/A or Parked rows as Out of scope. Set from the editor's own right-click menu. Once set, a small colored glyph shows on that node in the editor and in PDF exports. In the editor, clicking the glyph filters the tree to that marker — showing every matching node, its full subtree, and its ancestors back to the root (dimmed, so they read as "here's where it lives" rather than more matches); a filter bar appears with a × to clear it. Right-click the glyph to clear the marker itself instead. A marker filter and a tag filter can both be active together — matching nodes must satisfy both (tag matching itself stays a plain per-node check, unlike the marker filter's subtree behavior).
  • Right-clicking empty space — editor canvas, file explorer, status bar, tab bar, or app bar — opens a separate, smaller menu of chrome-level actions, not the node menu above. Navigate it with ↓ / ↑ and Enter, same as the category picker above, or hover with a mouse — both move the same highlight. Editor canvas: switch theme and Collapse all/Expand all sit in the menu itself; a "More…" item opens a second menu at the same spot for the rest — hide/show file explorer, and Settings. File Explorer: switch theme, hide file explorer, Settings. Status bar: switch theme, Settings. Tab bar: switch theme, new document, close current tab, Settings. App bar: switch theme, hide/show file explorer, and "Declutter app bar" — which hides the title field, file explorer toggle, and the Documents/Templates buttons, but deliberately never hides Settings — hiding it would remove your only way back in. Every hide action here shows an Undo toast, same pattern as Quick Assist's own toggles. The toolbar, tab bar, status bar and app bar can't be hidden (zen mode hides the toolbar and tab bar while it's on)
  • Backlinks — while editing a node, type @ to mention another node by name; a dropdown filters as you type, pick with mouse or arrow keys + Enter. The reference renders as a clickable link that jumps to the target. Deleting a referenced node removes its links from all other nodes automatically
  • Tags — select a node and click the tag icon in the toolbar or right-click → Tags to open the tag popover. Existing document tags appear as chips to toggle; type a new name and press Enter to add. Tags render as #chips on the node. Click a chip in the tree to filter to that tag; click again or × to clear. Multi-select: toolbar button applies to all selected nodes
  • Checkboxes — click the toolbar button to toggle a node as a checkbox. Or type [ ] / [x] at the start of a node while editing — it auto-converts on commit. Click the box to check/uncheck. Parent checkbox nodes with checkbox children show a 2/5 progress badge; checking all children auto-checks the parent. Checked nodes are struck through and dimmed. Multi-select supported
  • Heading shortcut — type # through ###### (1 to 6 of them) followed by a space at the very start of a node, then finish editing — same auto-convert-on-commit as checkboxes above, and sets the node's real heading level (the same field the Heading toolbar button sets), stripping the markdown prefix. Caps at H6, matching the toolbar's own options — #Text with no space, or seven or more #, doesn't convert
  • Right-click a node → More → Insert above / Insert below / Add child (Ctrl/Cmd + Enter also adds a child)
  • Tab / Shift + Tab → indent / outdent
  • Right-click a node → More → Duplicate → duplicate node / subtree, with its own copies of the note, tables, images, Q&A, remarks and diagrams (copy/paste brings them along too)
  • Alt + ↑ / ↓ → move (or right-click → More → Move up / Move down)
  • Drag a row → drop above/below to reorder, or onto the middle of another row to nest as its child. Dragging any node that's part of a multi-selection moves the whole selection together
  • Right-click a node with children → More → Sort children (A → Z, Z → A, or by depth — shallowest subtree first)
  • Right-click the open document's tab → Sort top-level nodes (A → Z, Z → A, or by depth) — the same tab menu has Version history and Clear all nodes (asks first; Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes it)

Tagging

  • Select a node and click the tag icon (toolbar Insert group) or right-click → Tags to open the tag popover. Existing document tags appear as chips to toggle; type a new name and press Enter to add. Remove a tag from a node by toggling its chip off in the popover
  • Tags render as #chips directly on the node row. Click a chip in the tree to filter the entire tree to that tag; click the chip again or the × to clear the filter
  • Multi-select: select several nodes, then click the tag icon — the popover applies to all selected nodes at once. Tags already on all selected nodes appear toggled on; tags on only some appear in an indeterminate state

@ Mentions & Backlinks

  • While editing a node, type @ to mention another node by name; a dropdown filters as you type — pick with mouse or arrow keys + Enter. The reference is saved as [[Node name]] and renders as a clickable link that jumps to the target node
  • Deleting a referenced node automatically removes its [[mention]] links from all other nodes
  • Turning the feature off (Settings → Panels → Backlinks) suppresses the @ dropdown. Existing [[mentions]] in node text still render as clickable links regardless — they navigate on click even when the feature is off

Focus (zoom into a branch)

  • Right-click a node → Zoom in (or Ctrl/Cmd + ., or the zoom icon at the right end of the toolbar) → only that node and its descendants are shown. A breadcrumb bar appears above the editor showing the path back to the root; click any crumb to zoom out to that level
  • Exit focus with Ctrl/Cmd + ,, by clicking the same toolbar button again, or by clicking the root crumb in the breadcrumb bar
  • Focus state is saved with the document, the same way fold state is — closing and reopening it (even in a new session) returns to whatever branch was last focused
  • Turning the feature off (Settings → Editing → Focus) hides the zoom-in toolbar button and right-click action, and exits any active focus session immediately. Ctrl/Cmd + . also stops working while the feature is off

Hovering a node

  • The fold/unfold arrow (▾/▸) on any node with children turns into −/+ while you hover it, and clicking it works exactly the same either way
  • Hovering the tree connector or the leaf dot at the start of a node — not the label text — shows a themed tooltip with when it was created and last modified

Formatting

  • Ctrl/Cmd + B → bold
  • Ctrl/Cmd + I → italic
  • Ctrl/Cmd + U → underline
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + S → strike
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + H → highlight (caret next to it picks a color)
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F → text color (caret next to it picks a color)
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + 1–6 → apply Heading 1–6 to the selected node(s), independent of tree depth — pick from the dropdown next to Text color, or Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + 0 / re-clicking the same level to return to body text. Combines with bold/italic/underline/strike on top if you want further emphasis

Semantics

  • **Text** → bold — or select text and press Ctrl/Cmd+B to bold just that selection
  • __Text__ → italic — or select text and press Ctrl/Cmd+I to italicize just that selection
  • @Node name → Node name — backlink to another node; type @ while editing to pick from a list
  • [ ] task or [x] task → auto-converts to a checkbox node on commit
  • Tag icon in the toolbar or right-click → Tags → tag popover (toggle existing tags or add new ones)

AI Rewrite

  • button in the toolbar → rewrites the selected node; with multiple nodes selected, rewrites all of them in one batch; with text highlighted inside an editing node, rewrites just that selection
  • Right-click a node → Rewrite node is in the quick icon row (Rewrite selection, if multiple are selected)
  • button next to Rewrite, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + O → Generate outline (AI): describe a topic and it inserts an AI-generated nested outline into the current document — into a blank doc, or after the current selection; also available as "Generate with AI" on the blank-document screen. Uses the same provider/model/key as Rewrite (Settings → AI → Provider), but its own fixed instructions, not the customizable rewrite prompt
  • Batches larger than 30 nodes are sent in sequential chunks automatically, with a status toast showing progress (e.g. "Rewriting nodes 1–30…")
  • Sakura Hosted AI — Settings → AI → the "AI Mode" switch at the top → "Sakura Hosted AI", then sign in. No key to find or paste; Sakura's own credentials handle the request via a small Cloudflare Worker, capped by a daily per-account quota. The request text for that one call goes to Sakura's server and on to a third-party provider Sakura selects, not stored either way — see Settings → About → Privacy & data for the full picture. Selecting it collapses the panel down to just sign-in status — no model or key fields, since there's nothing to configure. Prefer your own key, or want usage with no daily cap? Flip the same switch to "Bring your own key" instead
  • Settings → AI → AI Mode → "Bring your own key" reveals the Provider dropdown, Model, and API Key fields (hidden entirely under Sakura Hosted AI) — choose a provider, paste the API key for it, then head to the Rewrite section to optionally customise the rewrite prompt. All AI features — Rewrite (node, selection, note and remark lines, To-Do tasks and subtasks), Auto-rewrite, Generate outline — share whichever AI Mode and provider/key is currently active. "Reset to default" next to the prompt box restores the original grammar-and-spelling-only wording; "Rephrase" swaps in a different canned prompt that's allowed to restructure sentences and vary wording, not just correct errors — both replace the box's contents and save immediately, the same way, so review before relying on either. There's only one active prompt: switching to Rephrase also changes what Auto-rewrite on commit does, if it's on, since auto-rewrite always uses whichever prompt is currently active. "Reset AI settings", at the bottom of the "Bring your own key" section, restores your provider and model choices, clears every saved key, and also resets the shared rewrite prompt — want just the prompt reset, without touching your keys? Use "Reset to default" next to the prompt box instead. Switching AI Mode back and forth remembers whichever BYOK provider you were last on for the rest of the session (not saved across a reload if you leave on Sakura Hosted AI)
  • Auto-rewrite on commit (Settings → AI → Auto-rewrite on commit, off by default) — runs Rewrite automatically on a node as soon as you finish editing it, no manual click needed. Only text typed by hand counts: if any part of an edit session came from a paste or drop (checked via the browser's own paste/drop signal on that edit), that node is skipped for auto-rewrite on that commit — paste it, then use the manual Rewrite button if you want AI on it. Committing a node with no actual text change (e.g. clicking in and back out without editing) is also skipped — it doesn't re-queue nodes that haven't changed. It doesn't send one request per node: committed nodes are queued and sent as a single batched request once either an idle pause passes or enough nodes have queued up, whichever comes first — both the pause length (1-300s, default 120s) and the queue size (2-50, default 5) are configurable in Settings, not fixed — built this way specifically to avoid exhausting provider rate limits during continuous note-taking. A small ✦ dot appears next to any node currently queued (or mid-batch, waiting on the response) — click that dot to pull just that node back out of the queue before it's sent — separate from the status bar chip, which shows the overall off / idle / queued-count-with-a-live-countdown / paused / rewriting state and doubles as the control itself: click it to turn auto-rewrite on or off directly (see below for what clicking does instead while it's paused), right-click it for its settings (exclusions, minimum word count, idle pause, queue size). The countdown ticks down to the batch's send time and resets to the full idle-pause value every time another node joins the queue — a fresh edit means a fresh wait, not a shorter one. Both the queued count and the countdown are independently hideable from the chip (Settings → AI → Auto-rewrite on commit, below the queue-size setting) if either feels like more detail than you want at a glance — the chip still distinguishes "something's queued" from idle even with both turned off, just without the numbers; the tooltip on hover always shows the full detail regardless of what the chip itself displays. Exclusions (checkboxes, headings, [[backlinks]]/`code` syntax) and the minimum word count are each independently configurable checkboxes in Settings, not fixed. Needs a usable active provider to do anything — for a BYOK provider that means a key configured above; for Sakura Hosted AI, being signed in. If that's not the case right now — no key set, Secure Storage is locked so the saved one can't be read, or hosted is selected and you're signed out — the chip turns red and shows "paused," queued nodes are held rather than discarded, and the batch sends automatically the moment the provider becomes usable again (e.g. right after unlocking, or right after signing in) rather than waiting for the next edit to retrigger it. Clicking the chip while paused acts as the fix — unlocks Secure Storage directly if that's the cause, or jumps to the key field in Settings if not. That's separate from the retry-exhaustion case: if it fails three times in a row with a key that is available (e.g. an expired key), it turns itself off and tells you why, rather than silently retrying forever. Switching documents discards anything still queued rather than rewriting into the wrong document. Nodes created by Generate outline, paste-a-tree, and OPML import are never queued for auto-rewrite regardless of this setting — only nodes you type into interactively go through commitEdit at all
  • Built-in providers — seven BYOK providers ship with Sakura: Gemini (free), Groq (free, fast), Claude API, ChatGPT (OpenAI), OpenRouter (free models), Cerebras, and GitHub Models (free, needs your GitHub account). Cerebras's own free access varies by account and model — check their Billing tab if a request fails with a payment-required error. This is the complete, fixed list — Sakura doesn't support adding another provider. All need an API key — selecting a provider shows a direct link to where you get one. GitHub Models requires a GitHub personal access token with models:read scope; model IDs in the dropdown already include the required vendor prefix (e.g. openai/gpt-4o). These seven only show up under AI Mode → "Bring your own key" — Sakura Hosted AI needs no key at all and is the other AI Mode option, see the bullet above
  • Provider fallback — Settings → AI → Provider → Fallback order: enable the toggle to let Sakura automatically retry with the next checked provider when the active one fails — quota, rate limit, wrong model ID, or any other error. The active provider is always tried first; the list sets the retry order. Providers without a saved key are skipped automatically, and if none of the checked providers besides the active one have a key, a notice under the list says so directly rather than letting it fail silently the first time it's actually needed. A toast names both the failed provider and the one that succeeded (e.g. “Quota hit on Groq — rewritten with Gemini ✦” or “Error on Groq — rewritten with Gemini ✦”). The only error that does not trigger fallback is a bad API key (401) — that surfaces directly so you know to update it. Default order on a fresh install: Groq → Gemini → Cerebras → OpenRouter, with the first three enabled
  • Usage today — below the API key field, Sakura counts requests made to the currently selected provider today (and shows the count next to each provider in the Fallback order list once any requests are made). This is a local, best-effort counter — it resets on your computer's local calendar day, which can drift slightly from a provider's own reset clock (e.g. Gemini resets at midnight Pacific), and it isn't fetched from the provider itself. Treat it as a rough gauge of how much you've used a provider today, not an authoritative quota reading — check the provider's own dashboard (e.g. Google AI Studio) for the real number if it matters
  • Test key — the Test button next to Save sends a minimal request (asks the model to reply "OK") to confirm the currently typed or saved key actually works, without waiting for your next real Rewrite to find out. A toast reports success or the specific error. This check does not count toward the Usage today total above, since it's a connectivity check rather than real feature use

Utilities

  • Ctrl/Cmd + S → save now (kept in-app — doesn't trigger the browser's "Save Page As")
  • Export ▾ has two items: PDF and OPML. Both always include folded sections, whatever is collapsed in the outline editor; PDF also includes every note, code block, Q&A item, and remark, and OPML writes each node's note as its _note attribute. Copying nodes with Ctrl/Cmd+C likewise always includes folded children
  • Import ▾ (next to Export ▾) → OPML imports an .opml outline file as a new document
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + D → insert the date/time (also in Quick Insert, Ctrl/Cmd + Space, and right-click → More → Insert date/time)
  • Shortcuts that double as OS/browser bindings can occasionally be intercepted before they reach the page — if one doesn't fire, the matching button or menu item always works

Maximize / Zen mode

  • ⤢ floating button bottom-right of the editor, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + E, toggles zen mode; Esc exits it. Zen mode hides the file explorer, the toolbar, and the tab bar, and switches the browser to fullscreen (the same as pressing F11). The app bar and status bar always stay visible
  • Exiting fullscreen — Esc, F11, or the browser's own control — exits zen mode at the same time, so the two never end up out of sync
  • The header's own sidebar-toggle button (▤) keeps working normally throughout zen mode, so you can always open or close the file explorer manually for that session; leaving zen mode brings it back if zen mode hid it

Export as PDF

  • Export ▾ → PDF renders the document straight from its current content and opens the browser's print dialog — choose "Save as PDF" there. No separate step needed first
  • The PDF always contains the whole document: folded sections, notes and code blocks, Q&A, and remarks are all included, each right under the node it belongs to
  • Headings come from the Heading 1–6 style you apply in the editor (Format toolbar, next to Text color) — not from tree depth. A node with no heading style of its own renders as plain body text; [Bracketed] section markers render as section headings
  • A Contents page built from headings (levels 1–2) and [Section] markers is included at the start of every PDF export. Every page gets a footer with the export date and "Page N of M"
  • Settings → Data & backup → Export & copy: "Cover page" adds a title page before the contents page; "PDF branding" adds a small mark on the cover page and in every page's bottom-right corner (on by default, with your own text if you set one); "Use accent color in exports" picks between your accent color and a fixed color
  • Notes render as their real rich content (images, lists, links) in exports, not the small dot from the editor

Large trees

  • Click ▾/▸ → fold / unfold subtree
  • ← / → → collapse / expand selected
  • Ctrl/Cmd + F → search this tree; Ctrl/Cmd + H → search and replace (Replace / Replace all, undoable)
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + C / ▶ at the right end of the toolbar → collapse all (folds every top-level section)
  • Same shortcut / same button again → expand all — it's a single toggle, the icon flips to show which one it'll do next
  • Both cover inline objects too: Expand all opens every note, Q&A, remark and diagram under its row and unfolds tables and images; Collapse all closes and folds them. While anything is still closed, the button offers Expand all

Documents & folders

  • button in file explorer header → new folder; button → new document (unfiled); or Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + N from anywhere
  • Hover a folder → ＋ creates a document already filed there; ✎ renames it; deletes it (subfolders move up a level, documents move to Unfiled — Undo appears briefly after deleting)
  • Right-click a folder → new document or new subfolder here, rename, or delete
  • Right-click a document → rename, duplicate, move to a folder, or move to Trash
  • Click ✎ / ⧉ / icons on a document row → rename / duplicate / move to Trash; the folder-icon button moves it via a dropdown list
  • Click a document's icon (left of its name) → pick from a small set of icons to mark it visually, or "Use default icon" to clear it back to the plain page icon. Purely visual, doesn't affect the document's content
  • Click a document's or folder's name → switch to it / expand it
  • Folders can be nested: drag a folder onto another folder's top or bottom edge to reorder it as a sibling there, or onto the middle to nest it inside
  • Drag a document onto a folder (or "Unfiled") to file it there; drag it onto another document to reorder within that folder/Unfiled
  • / buttons by "Documents" → collapse all / expand all folders (only shown once a folder exists)
  • Ctrl/Cmd-click a document to multi-select; Shift-click selects a range. A bar appears to move or trash the whole selection at once
  • Deleting a document (or a selection of them) moves it to Trash, a collapsible section at the very bottom of the file explorer — out of the way since it's rarely needed, same as most apps put it. It's not gone. Each item there shows when it was trashed, with buttons to restore it or delete it forever. A toast with "Undo" also appears right after trashing, for a quick reversal without opening Trash at all. Settings → Trash controls how long items sit there before being purged automatically (default 7 days; "Forever" turns off auto-purge so only "Empty Trash" removes anything). Header search (Ctrl/Cmd + K) skips Trash by default — turn on Settings → Trash → "Include Trash in search" to have it surface matches there too (across documents, node text, Notes, tags, and the Pad alike), clearly marked "In Trash"; clicking one reveals it in the Trash section rather than opening it directly, since restoring is a deliberate choice
  • Searching the file explorer keeps folders visible (showing only matching documents and subfolders, force-expanded) but disables drag-and-drop while a search is active; it only matches document names — for text inside documents, use the header search (Ctrl/Cmd + K) instead
  • The file explorer's filter box is hidden by default since the header search now covers the same ground; bring it back via the icon next to "Documents", or Settings → Bars & Menus → File Explorer → Filter box
  • Drag the thin strip at the file explorer's right edge to resize it
  • Version history (right-click a document in the file explorer, or its tab, → "Version history") keeps automatic checkpoints of a document's past content — not full version control, just lightweight snapshots. A version is captured right before it would otherwise be overwritten, but only once every ~10 minutes of active editing at most, and only if something actually changed, so it won't flood with near-duplicates from every autosave tick. Capped at the last 10 per document, oldest dropped first. "Save a version now" in that panel adds one immediately, useful right before a big rewrite. Restoring an older version is itself non-destructive — whatever was there gets saved as a version first, so restoring is never a one-way trip
  • If the same document is open as the active one in two tabs or windows of this browser at once (easy to do by accident — duplicating a tab, browser session restore, opening the file twice), a banner appears the moment the other one saves a change, since otherwise whichever tab saves last would silently win with no warning. "Reload latest" discards anything unsaved here and pulls in the other tab's version; dismissing it just clears the banner — your edits here are kept either way, and the other tab gets the same warning in reverse once you save. Documents open here only in the background (not the one on screen) refresh silently instead, since there's nothing unsaved there to protect. This only applies within one browser — a completely different browser, or a different device, never shares storage and can't collide

Sharing & sync

  • Signing in (Google or email, from the account button top-right) syncs your documents, folders, and settings to your account, so they follow you to another browser or device. Fully optional — everything keeps working locally without it, and nothing here requires an account except sharing a document with someone else, which needs both people signed in
  • Profile visibility (Settings → Account, or the Private/Public badge in the account menu itself — either one toggles the same setting) — Private by default. Setting it to Public lets someone find your account by typing your exact email or name when sharing a document with you; Private means your account genuinely can't be found that way, not just hidden behind an extra step. Your name and photo only ever show up in someone's search results once it's set to Public
  • Share a document — a "Share" chip appears under the title (next to Status/Author/Link) once you're signed in and a document is open; right-click a document in the file explorer → "Share…" does the same, switching to it first if it isn't already open. Type a name or email to search — results only ever include accounts set to Public, shown with their photo/initial, name, and email so you can tell you've got the right person. Click a result to share immediately with whichever access level ("Can view" / "Can edit") is currently selected. The same panel lists everyone who currently has access, with a dropdown to change their role and a × to remove them, at any time
  • View vs. edit access — a document shared as "Can view" is read-only for that person: their changes won't actually save even if the outline lets them type, since the save itself is rejected without edit access. "Can edit" allows real changes, which sync back to your account the same as your own edits do
  • Shared — a collapsible section in the file explorer, right after your own documents, listing everything other accounts have shared with you (who shared it, and your access level). Click one to open it as a regular tab. Reopening after closing it or reloading the page means going back to the Shared section and opening it again — a shared document doesn't stay in your tab strip across a reload the way your own documents do
  • The bell icon next to the account button shows notifications for sharing activity — a new share, an access-level change, or your access being removed. A dot shows how many are unread; clicking a share or access-level notification marks it read and jumps straight to that document
  • Who's viewing a document — a green "N is here" chip appears next to the Share button while someone else (owner or another collaborator) has the same shared document open, so you're not editing blind. It only shows up on documents that are actually shared with at least one other person

Tabs

  • Click a document in the file explorer, or the + at the end of the tab strip → opens it as a tab. Switching tabs keeps each one's undo history, scroll position, and selection independent — it doesn't reset like a plain document switch would
  • Double-click a tab → rename it
  • on a tab, or Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + W → closes the active tab only; the document itself isn't deleted and stays in the file explorer. Closing the last tab leaves the editor empty rather than reopening another document
  • Drag a tab left or right to reorder the strip
  • ▾ at the right of the tab strip → search all open tabs by name; ↑ / ↓ + Enter to jump, or click a result
  • "Reopen tabs on launch" (a Quick Assist toggle — search "reopen tabs") controls whether your open tabs come back next time, or you start with just one

Backing up your data

  • Signing in (see "Sharing & sync" above) syncs your documents continuously to your account — a live, off-device copy that needs no extra setup. Signed out, backing up is manual: nothing leaves this browser unless you run Backup yourself
  • Everything is stored locally in the browser, scoped to this exact file. Opening a different copy or a newer version of this file starts with empty storage — that's a browser limitation, not a bug
  • Settings → Data → Backup all data → saves every document, folder, To-Do, and setting to a single file you keep. Restore from backup reads one back — it replaces everything currently in the app, which is why both live only in Settings rather than as one-click shortcuts. The header's Export ▾ and Import ▾ buttons are for the current document only (PDF, OPML) — Backup/Restore cover all your data
  • Settings → Data → Undo last restore → appears only after you've used Restore — a snapshot of whatever was in the app right before that restore, in case the file you picked turns out to have been the wrong one. One level deep: it holds only what was there before your most recent restore
  • Settings → Data → Secure Storage → optional, encrypts AI provider keys at rest (AES-GCM, passphrase-derived key) instead of storing them as plain text — in this browser and in local backup files. The passphrase itself is never stored anywhere; unlocking derives the key fresh each time, and it only lives in memory for that session — reload the page and you'll need to unlock again to use your own AI keys. There's no recovery if you forget it. Turning it off writes everything back as plain text. Once it's set up, a status-bar chip shows when it's locked and unlocks it in one click; right-click the chip to jump to the full Secure Storage controls instead. Unlocking also automatically resumes Auto-rewrite on commit if it was paused waiting on a key
  • Recommended: back up all data before switching to a new version of this file, then restore right after opening it
  • Settings → Data → Reset to default settings → restores appearance/behavior preferences only (theme, accent, text size, etc.); your documents and AI settings aren't touched

Notes

  • Every node can hold a plain-text note, shown and edited directly underneath the node in the outline itself — there's no separate panel to open. Add or open one via the toolbar ( Note button), right-click → More → Note, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + N
  • A node with a note shows a small chat-bubble dot — click it to expand the note as its own line directly under the node, editable right there; click again to collapse it
  • The note line grows automatically as you type multiple lines. Backspace at the start of an empty note deletes it
  • Right-click the note line for AI Rewrite (rewrites the note's current text) or Delete note

Thread (comments and questions)

  • Every node has one thread: the conversation about it, kept right under the row as a flat list in time order, oldest first. Each entry shows its author (a colored initials avatar plus the name; each person in a document gets their own color), the time it was written, and the text. An entry is a Comment or a Question
  • Right-click any node (or Insert, or Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+M) → Thread… opens the node's thread with the cursor on a new reply line. Type and press Enter to add the entry (Shift+Enter for a new line, Esc to close). While you type, Ask makes it a question. At rest a thread shows no reply box — hover it for + Reply. What you type is kept if you move to another row
  • The reply line writes as the last author used — click the name (Robin ▾) to reply as someone else, e.g. when you note what a colleague said in a call. Click an entry's name or time to correct it
  • A question carries a Question chip, in your accent colour, until it's answered; then it reads “· question, answered” in grey. An answer that comes a few entries after its question quotes it (“↳ Does it…”). Answer it from the reply line with Yes or No (plus anything you typed — a bare Yes/No takes one line), or right-click a reply → Mark as the answer. Right-click the question → Won't answer closes it without one; "Reopen question" takes that back
  • Status: right-click an entry → Agreed, Follow-up or Out of scope marks it (shown as quiet text, e.g. “· agreed”, on that entry). The latest one is the thread's status, and it is the row's marker — the one place the status is shown in colour. Clicking a marker on a row adds it to the thread by the current author (Follow-up also opens the reply line); clearing it takes it back. The reply line has Follow-up, and Agree while the thread is a follow-up — each adds an entry by the current author
  • Decision: right-click the entry where something was decided → Mark as decision puts a Decision chip on it (in the PDF too), and the thread's header says “· Decision” (click it to jump there). It doesn't change the row's marker
  • Right-click an entry for Reply, Make it a question / comment, Mark as decision, its status (the row-marker icons, current one highlighted — click it again to clear), Rewrite with AI (when AI is on) or Delete; an entry emptied and left, or emptied with Backspace, is removed
  • A speech-bubble icon appears on a node with a thread — click it to show or hide the thread inline. The thread is grey; the icon takes your accent colour and shows a count while questions are still open
  • A thread longer than four entries shows its latest three; the header's “show N earlier” shows the rest
  • Always included in PDF exports: the whole thread prints right after its node as a transcript — a "Thread · N" header, then every entry with its author, time (the date once per day), Yes/No and status as text, the avatars joined by a faint line. The status prints once, on the row's marker. The outline shows the thread the same way; click its header to hide it
  • Deleting a node deletes its thread too (and its note, tables, images and diagrams); Undo brings it back. Only diagrams can't be undone, so deleting one asks first, with a red warning
  • Older documents open converted: Q&A linked to a node becomes a question in that node's thread with its answer as a reply; follow-ups become statuses and decisions become Decision chips (Agreed), and the row marker is lined up with them. Q&A section headers and questions not linked to a node stay as they were and print in the PDF's closing Q&A list

Tables

  • Right-click a node → Add table… opens a size picker: hover or use the arrow keys to choose up to 8 columns × 8 rows (the readout shows columns × rows), then click or press Enter; Esc cancels. The new table has a header row and opens for editing with its first header cell selected
  • Click a table to edit its cells; Esc or a click outside finishes. Each editing session is one Ctrl/Cmd+Z step
  • While editing: Tab / Shift + Tab move to the next / previous cell (Tab in the last cell adds a row), Enter moves down (adding a row at the bottom), Shift + Enter starts a new line in the cell, ↑ / ↓ on a cell's first / last line move to the cell above / below
  • Right-click a cell for: add row above/below, add column left/right, move row up/down, move column left/right, sort A → Z / Z → A (numbers, percentages, amounts and dates sort by value), turn the header row on/off, align the column left/center/right, and delete row/column/table
  • Paste a range copied from Excel or Google Sheets into a table you're editing: it fills the cells from the caret and adds rows and columns as needed
  • Columns of numbers right-align automatically unless you've set the column's alignment; alignment shows the same in the PDF
  • A chart or Cards figure stays a chart when clicked — double-click it, or right-click → Edit data, to edit its table
  • A table shown as a table displays clean: horizontal rules only, a quiet header, and a faint "–" in empty cells. Clicking in to edit shows the full grid
  • Right-click a table → Group rows shows each repeated first-column value once, spanning its rows (a "code (name)" value shows as a bold code over its name). Display only — editing still shows every row

Images

  • Screenshots and pictures belong to a node as their own objects (not inside its note): a node can hold any number, shown as a compact row of thumbnails directly under it, each with its caption underneath
  • Add them by pasting a screenshot (Ctrl/Cmd+V) while the node is selected, being edited, or its note line has the cursor; by dropping image files onto the node; or right-click → Add image… (under "More" by default) to pick one or more files
  • New images are shrunk to at most 1600px on the long side and saved as WebP (JPEG where the browser can't make WebP), which keeps documents small enough to sync; SVGs and animated GIFs are kept exactly as they are
  • Click a thumbnail to open the enlarged viewer: edit the caption under the picture, step through the node's images with ←/→ or the side arrows, pick a display size (Auto, Small, Medium, Full — used in the viewer and in PDF exports), or Delete it. Esc or clicking outside closes it
  • Mark up in the viewer (or M) to draw on a screenshot without changing the picture: rectangle (R), arrow (A), translucent highlighter (H), and text labels (T — click, type, Enter; double-click a label to edit it), in six colours. The select tool (V) moves a mark (drag, or the arrow keys), recolours it, or deletes it (Delete). Undo/redo inside the editor with Ctrl/Cmd+Z / Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z; Clear markings removes them all. Esc backs out one step at a time; Done finishes. Marks stay in place at any display size, show on the thumbnails and in PDF exports, and a whole marking session is one step of the document's undo
  • Click a caption under a thumbnail to edit it right there (Enter saves, Esc cancels). Right-click a thumbnail for Open, Add/Edit caption, Size (Auto, Small, Medium, Full), Mark up…, Move left/right, or Delete image; drag a thumbnail onto another to reorder. Everything is undoable with Ctrl/Cmd+Z
  • A small picture dot appears on a node with images — click it to fold or unfold the thumbnails. A folded branch's "+N hidden" badge mentions images inside it
  • Copying nodes (Ctrl/Cmd+C) carries their images when pasted back into Sakura; duplicating a node copies them too. PDF exports show each image under its node with its caption; OPML can't hold images, so they're left out there
  • Pictures that older versions kept inside a note move into the node's images automatically the first time the document opens — the note's text stays as it was

Diagrams

  • A real draw.io editor, embedded directly — not a static image. Every diagram belongs to a node in the outline and shows up as a small preview card directly under it; a node can hold any number of diagrams
  • Right-click a node → Add diagram… to create one already linked to that node — it opens full-screen in draw.io immediately. Click a diagram's preview card (or the small open icon next to its title) to reopen it the same way; the card shows a live thumbnail once it's been saved at least once, and its title can be renamed right on the card
  • Right-click a node → Generate diagram (listed under "More") turns that node's whole subtree into a rough draw.io diagram automatically, linked to the same node. Meant as a fast first draft to refine by hand afterward in draw.io, not a finished diagram. Caps out at 60 nodes/10 levels deep per generation to stay readable; generate a smaller branch separately if yours is bigger than that.
  • Generate opens a review screen first — every node in scope, with its proposed shape (plain box, a specific shape like Decision/Datastore/External, or "Edge label"/"Passthrough" to fold it into the diagram rather than draw its own box), whether it's a titled Container, whether its children form a Sequence (chained, vs. fanned out independently), and Sequence direction (vertical/horizontal). Everything's pre-filled with a best guess from the outline's own structure — adjust anything that guessed wrong, select multiple rows for the bulk toolbar at the top, then Generate. Classification is remembered per diagram (not on the node, and never as a document tag — nothing here shows up as a tag chip anywhere else), so regenerating the same scope later reopens pre-filled with whatever you set last time instead of starting over.
  • Only changes saved inside draw.io itself are kept — its own Save button, or Ctrl/Cmd+S, while the editor is open. Closing the full-screen editor (the × button, or Esc) always asks you to confirm you've saved, since there's no way to force a save from outside draw.io's own UI
  • Multiple pages/tabs within one diagram: draw.io's own page tabs (bottom-left of the editor) work as usual, and every page's content is kept in full when you save and reopen. But the thumbnail, and the figure shown in PDF exports, can only ever show one page — whichever was active in the editor at the moment you last saved. (An earlier version of this tried exporting every page individually behind the scenes; that turned out to actively corrupt the live diagram — deleting a page from it — so it was reverted. Nothing unsafe is attempted here anymore.) A "N pages" badge appears in the full-screen editor's header as a reminder when this applies. If you want more than one page to actually appear in the document, create them as separate diagrams, each under its own node, instead of using pages within one diagram
  • Give it a title in the field at the top of the full-screen editor; the anchor button next to it moves the diagram under a different node. Choosing "Not linked to a node" there detaches it — an unlinked diagram has no preview card to reopen it from, so only do that if you mean to set it aside
  • A linked diagram appears as a large figure directly under its node in PDF exports — same treatment as a note image marked "Feature as diagram" elsewhere in Sakura, so there's no visible difference between the two workflows in the output
  • A small accent-colored square-cluster dot appears next to a node with a linked diagram — click it to show or hide that node's diagram preview cards inline. The same icon appears next to a folded node's "+N hidden" badge when a diagram is linked somewhere inside its collapsed subtree
  • The full-screen editor's header has Duplicate (same drawing, same status, same node link, titled "(original title) (copy)" — a pure data copy, so it's instant) and Delete (removes the diagram and its node link; the toast's Undo button brings it back for 5 seconds — deleting never touches the node itself)
  • Each diagram has a status — Draft, In Progress, Review, or Final — shown as a small colored pill in the full-screen editor's header. Click it to cycle to the next status. Purely organizational — nothing else in Sakura reads it (it's not exported or shown in Preview)
  • Each diagram has a private, one-line note — a reminder to yourself, e.g. "needs sign-off before this is final." Type directly into the small field in the full-screen editor's header — no popup, no separate edit step. Enter or clicking away saves it, Esc discards whatever was typed since it was last saved. Never shown in PDF exports or anywhere outside that editor
  • Diagrams and Q&A are both included in Sakura's Version History (right-click the open document's tab, or a document in the file explorer → Version history) — restoring an older version restores them alongside the outline text. A restored diagram's thumbnail is blank until it's reopened and saved once in draw.io, which regenerates it automatically; the diagram's actual content isn't affected, only the cached preview image. Restoring a version recorded before this existed leaves diagrams/Q&A exactly as they currently are, rather than guessing or wiping them — but if one of those diagrams is anchored to a node that only exists in the newer state you're restoring away from, it becomes unlinked once the outline rolls back (the data itself isn't deleted). The "Version restored" toast names how many diagrams this happened to, if any, so it's never silent
  • Generate — builds a rough flowchart directly from the outline instead of a blank canvas: the right-clicked node's subtree becomes a real, editable draw.io diagram linked under that node (capped at 60 nodes / 10 levels — a toast asks for a smaller section if you're over that). Layout, sizing, color, and the diagram's XML are always built by deterministic code — AI is only ever asked for a small, whitelisted classification of that same outline (never coordinates, never XML, never a restructured hierarchy), which the deterministic renderer then draws:
    • Structure — boxes tile top-down following the outline's own hierarchy. A node whose children are all childless (a flat list of steps rather than genuine sub-branches) renders as a single vertical chain with sequential arrows instead of fanning out sideways — keeps a long flat step-list narrow rather than blowing out the canvas width, and reads as one continuous sequence rather than alternate paths. That whole chain (the node plus every one of its steps) also gets a background card drawn behind it, tinted to a lighter version of that group's own color rather than one fixed neutral — a pink actor group and a blue UI group each read as their own section, not both sharing the same generic card — so a labeled group of steps ("Webshop Layer" and everything under it, say) reads as one section on the page itself, its own text sitting directly on that card as the section's title rather than getting a redundant box of its own. If those steps are themselves explicitly numbered too ("1 · Simulate order", "2 · Calculate weight", ...), the chain lays out left to right in a row instead of the usual top-to-bottom column — same "these are ordered stages" signal, one level deeper. A node with a real mix of children (some with sub-detail, some without) still fans out normally — unless every one of those children is explicitly numbered ("1. Webshop Layer", "2. ERP Layer", ...), in which case they're read as ordered stages of one flow rather than alternate branches and stack top to bottom instead, each stage's own full subtree rendered normally beneath it, connected from wherever that stage's own content actually ends (not skipping over it) to the next stage's start. Tag that parent node horizontal (or row) to lay those stages out left to right instead — same idea as the numbered-leaf case above, just for stages that still have their own sub-detail, where structure alone can't tell "these are still parallel enough to sit in a row" apart from "these are sequential phases, stack them" (a top-level phase sequence and a same-shaped row of sub-steps look identical on paper). Each stage keeps its own subtree laid out normally beneath it either way — the tag only changes whether stages sit side by side or stacked. All-or-nothing: every sibling in the group has to be numbered for this to kick in, so one numbered aside among ordinary children doesn't pull the whole group into sequence mode by accident. Numbering style is flexible — "1.", "1)", "1:", "1 · ", "1 - " all count, since people number lists differently and the character itself isn't the meaningful part
    • Color — a branch color cycles through 8 hues at every genuine fan-out in the tree, not just the top level, so a real branch point several levels deep (not just the outline's own top-level headings) still gets visually distinct paths with zero AI involved; a chain group's steps stay one uniform color on purpose. An explicit node marker (Confirmed/Issue/Parked/Follow-up/N-A — each its own hue) outranks that, and a node's first tag outranks plain branch color — a tag deterministically hashes to one of 8 reserved hues, so the same tag text always recolors the same way without any keyword list to set up first. All three carry down to untagged, unmarked descendants. Once AI has classified anything in this diagram (see below), a node it left unclassified switches from its branch color to a neutral gray instead — a branch hue has no legend entry to explain it, so once other colors on the page do mean something, an unexplained one would read as a mistake rather than "nothing special here"
    • Box size — width grows with the (possibly-shortened) label up to a cap, and only grows tall enough for two wrapped lines if the label actually needs them, rather than every box defaulting to the same fixed size. A decision diamond gets extra width/height on top of that (a rhombus's angled edges leave much less usable interior than a box's), plus a much tighter label-length budget than every other shape, since even the extra sizing isn't enough room for a full sentence
    • AI's job — one JSON call for the whole scope classifies which nodes are a UI/frontend step, a service call, middleware/integration, a backend process step, an actual persisted data store (kept distinct from an ordinary backend step — only a table/database/record gets the data-store cylinder), an external system, an actor, a genuine decision fork, a pure aside/caveat that isn't a step at all, or a branch that's explicitly out of scope of whatever's being described — each with its own fixed color and, where it helps, its own shape (diamond, cylinder, dashed, dotted). It can also flag a trigger node whose resulting outcomes are written as its siblings rather than its children (something the outline's own hierarchy has no way to connect on its own) and draw that connection as an extra edge, without changing the layout at all. A results-into-two-genuine-paths pattern is usually clearer expressed by nesting the outline itself that way in the first place, though — that's deterministic and doesn't depend on the model noticing anything, where an AI-suggested edge is inherently probabilistic and won't fire on every run. Every one of these is validated against the actual outline structure before it's trusted — a claimed decision only renders as a diamond if the node genuinely has 2+ children in the real tree, regardless of how the model read its own wording, and any classification outside a fixed whitelist is silently dropped. Genuinely fanning/parallel content (rare — most content that touches multiple systems is still a linear sequence, just one that hops between them) can additionally switch the whole diagram to a layered, swimlane-style layout instead. No AI key configured, a locked vault, a provider error, or a response that fails validation all fall back to the plain deterministic version above instead of blocking the diagram or leaving it half-classified — the Generate button spins for the duration of the call so a slower provider still has a visible in-progress state, and the toast afterward says whether AI classification actually applied this run or not
    • Tags — a node tagged decision, database (or db/datastore), excluded, ui, service, middleware, backend, external, actor, or note (a few spelling variants work too — see the source for the full list) sets that node's box type directly, the same shapes AI classification can produce — worth having even when AI didn't run at all, or when AI's own guess should be overridden for a specific node. An explicit tag always wins over whatever AI separately classified that node as. decision only sticks if the node genuinely has 2+ children, same structural guard AI's own decision classification uses, so a stale tag can't produce a diamond with no actual fork under it
    • Edge labels — a node tagged edge-label, placed as a sibling directly between two other nodes at the same outline level, contributes its own text as a label on the arrow connecting those two neighbors instead of becoming a box itself — useful for annotating a transition ("Passes: freight group & qty", "Returns: pricing values") the way a real system-integration diagram would. It never counts toward the 60-node cap and never gets its own layout slot; delete it (or remove the tag) to drop the label again
    • Only categories actually present on the page get a legend entry, drawn to the top-right of the diagram — never a static list of every possible category
    • Generating again for the same node offers to regenerate that diagram in place rather than adding a duplicate — confirms first, since it discards anything changed since inside draw.io; declining leaves the existing one untouched
    • Meant as a rough first draft to refine by hand afterward, not a finished diagram

To-Dos

  • An app-level task list — not tied to any document or node. One shared list across your whole workspace
  • Open it from the Hub button in the app bar, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + T; the same shortcut closes it again, and it switches straight to this tab if the panel is already open on a different one
  • Floating and draggable by its header; drag the thin strip on its left edge to resize its width (remembered between sessions). The button expands it full-screen the same way Note/Pad/Code do (temporarily overriding your custom width, restored when you leave full-screen)
  • Import loads a Sakura To-Dos file — a .json export from another Sakura session or shared by a colleague — adding its tasks to the end of your list with its own Undo toast; any task whose text matches one you already have is flagged (not skipped) in that toast, since text alone can't tell a real duplicate from two tasks that just happen to read the same. Export in the panel header → PDF prints the full list — Open then Completed — regardless of any active priority/status/due filter, so a filtered view never silently shortens the printout
  • Type a task and press Enter (or use the + button) to add it — the box grows as you type so long tasks stay readable. Shift+Enter inserts a line break instead of adding the task, both here and while editing an existing task's text
  • The clock icon next to Export opens Version History for the whole list — same idea as a document's Version History, kept separately since To-Dos isn't tied to any document. A version is saved automatically roughly every 10 minutes a change is made, or click "Save a version now" right before something risky. Restoring one replaces the current list (after saving a checkpoint of what was there first, so restoring is never itself destructive) — keeps the last 20 versions, app-wide
  • Checking a task off moves it straight to Completed, most-recently-finished first; unchecking sends it back to Open
  • The Open row shows how many open tasks match the current filter, with a magnifying-glass quick-find icon, sort and filter icons at its right edge. Sort covers Manual order, Priority, and Due date; filter narrows the list to one priority level (or tasks with none). Any icon turns accent-colored whenever it's off its default (or quick-find is open) so you can tell at a glance that something's active
  • Click the magnifying-glass icon to open quick-find and type to search task text, across both Open and Completed. Matches are highlighted and non-matching tasks are hidden entirely (not just dimmed), so the list actually shortens as you narrow it down — this composes with the priority filter, so a priority filter plus a search term shows only tasks matching both. Esc clears the search text first, then a second Esc (or clicking the icon again) closes it; the search always resets when you close the panel. Dragging to reorder still works correctly while filtered — a task dropped next to a visible neighbor lands there in the full list too, even if other hidden tasks sit between them. This searches task text only, live, within the panel — for a version that also opens the panel and jumps to the match from anywhere in the app, Quick Assist's todo: scope still does that
  • Turn on the select/reorder toggle (checklist icon in the header) to reveal each open task's drag handle, then drag it to reorder. Completed tasks aren't draggable — they're always ordered by completion time
  • Editing a task's text supports Ctrl/Cmd + Z / Ctrl/Cmd + Y to undo/redo that text edit — its own history, shared across all tasks (app-level, like the list itself) rather than per-task. This covers text edits only: adding, deleting, reordering, and completing tasks keep their existing in-panel Undo toasts instead
  • Click a task's own background — not its text, and not a checkbox/chip/button, all of which keep doing their own thing on click — to expand it and reveal a spark AI Rewrite button and a delete button on its chip row, alongside any unset priority/due/link/repeat placeholders. Click the row again to close it — collapsed rows show only the task text (plus any chips that already have a value), so a plain checklist-style task with nothing set takes up as little room as possible. Deleting shows an "Undo" toast, inside the panel itself, for a few seconds in case of a misclick — past that window, Version History (the clock icon) can still bring back a deleted task as part of restoring an earlier snapshot of the whole list
  • The Completed section header shows a Clear completed button whenever it has tasks (respecting the current priority filter) to remove them all in one action, with its own in-panel Undo toast — a batch counterpart to deleting one at a time. All To-Dos toasts (Undo prompts, export confirmation, AI rewrite errors) show inside the panel while it's open rather than the app's global toast, so acting on one never closes the panel
  • An overdue count badge appears on the To-Dos button itself whenever you have open, overdue tasks — visible without opening the panel
  • Priority, due date, and link chips sit below the task text. Priority cycles None → Low → Medium → High on click; due date shows "Today/Tomorrow" or the date, turning red once it's overdue. All three stay visible once set, and only reveal once you click the task to expand it while unset. Clicking the due date chip opens a small calendar popover with Today / Tomorrow / Next week presets up top for the common cases, month navigation for picking any other date, and a "Clear due date" option. Clicking the link chip opens a small popover with two tabs — Web link (an optional display-text field, a URL field, and Save; a bare domain or path is treated as an https:// link automatically) and Link to a node (a search box over your active documents — the same lookup Quick Assist and Global Search use — with results grouped into Documents, for linking the whole document, and Nodes, for one specific spot in it; leave the box empty to browse and pick a document without typing its title first), plus a Remove link option that clears whichever kind is set. A web-link chip shows your display text if you set one, or the link's hostname otherwise; a document-link chip shows the document's title with a plain document icon, and a node-link chip shows that node's own text with a small hierarchy icon, in place of the link-chain icon, so either reads as "jumps within Sakura" rather than "opens a website" — and both stay live, tracking the current title/text rather than a snapshot. Once any kind of link is attached, an open/jump button appears in the row's actions once it's expanded, next to Rewrite and Delete: for a web link it opens a new tab; for a document or node link it switches to that document if needed (scrolling to and briefly flashing the node, the same way backlinks do, when it's a node link specifically). If the node or document has since been deleted, the chip is shown with a dashed outline and clicking either it or the jump button gives a "That node no longer exists" (or "That document no longer exists") toast instead of failing silently
  • A task can either repeat or hold sub-tasks — never both at once. Click the Repeat chip to cycle None → Daily → Weekdays → Weekly; checking off a recurring task doesn't complete it, it just advances the due date to the next occurrence (a toast confirms the new date), so recurring tasks never pile up in Completed. Once a repeat is set, a small repeat glyph also shows on the due-date chip, even before you've set a due date, so it's clear at a glance that a task recurs
  • Click a task to expand it, then click Subtask to open an inline field — Enter adds it (Escape cancels), building a small nested checklist under the task with its own checkboxes, an n/300 character counter while typing, and a delete button per item on hover. A progress badge (e.g. "2/4") plus a collapse arrow appear once a task has any sub-tasks; the parent task's own checkbox is disabled and completes automatically the moment every sub-task is checked — you can't check the parent by hand while it has sub-tasks. Setting a repeat on a task removes its sub-tasks' ability to be added (and vice versa, adding a sub-task clears any repeat)
  • Right-click a task for a context menu — mark complete/open, duplicate the task, copy its text, move it to the top or bottom of the list, expand/collapse its sub-tasks, or delete it. Right-clicking directly on the task's own text, or on a sub-task row, falls through to the normal browser menu instead, so copy/paste and spellcheck still work there
  • Settings → To-Dos: auto-expire completed tasks after a set number of days, and cap how many completed tasks are kept (oldest drop first). The Completed section starts collapsed each time the panel opens — click its header to expand it
  • Typing @ directly in a task's text renders an inline chip: @name for an assignee, @date (ISO date, @today/@tomorrow, or a weekday like @fri) for a date reference, and @status (waiting/blocked/done/review) for status. A suggestion popup appears as you type, offering the date/status keywords plus any names you've already used as @name elsewhere — Arrow keys to navigate, Enter/Tab to accept, Escape to dismiss. These are colored text only — display convenience within the task text, not linked to the priority/due-date/link fields above
  • #tag renders as a colored tag chip — same autocomplete popup, suggesting tags you've already used. >remark renders everything from the > to the end of the line as a muted italic aside. Both are display only, same as @ tokens
  • Quick-find already searches the raw task text, so it matches #tags, @mentions, and remark text without any special handling — priority stays a separate structured field with its own dedicated filter
  • Quick Assist searches your tasks too — type a task's text, or scope it with todo: milk — and clicking a result opens the panel and flashes the match
Start with structure. Refine later.
